passage:
In history class, students studied a map showing borders from one hundred years ago. Many countries looked different.
A student asked, "Why do borders change if maps look so official?"
The teacher explained that borders can change because of wars, agreements, independence movements, and political decisions. A map may look fixed, but it is often a picture of power at one moment.
Students compared old maps with current ones. They saw that geography and history were deeply connected.
The lesson made maps feel less simple. Lines on paper can affect languages, families, trade, and identity. A border is thin on a map, but heavy in real life.
